ASTRA — Chemical transformation: From fragment storage to selective reaction control

1. A decisive limitation of the Fe(OEP) construction

The strongest new conclusion is that a stored Fe–alkyl intermediate does not automatically create useful programmable chemistry. Its value depends on what can be done after loading that cannot be achieved just as effectively by conventional feed scheduling.

The primary experimental foundation is sound within its scope. Pace and colleagues demonstrated Fe(I)(OEP) activation of primary alkyl electrophiles, accumulation of a primary Fe(III)–alkyl intermediate, and productive coupling with tertiary radicals under iron/photoredox conditions. The reaction also works with primary mesylates, not only alkyl bromides.

macmillan.princeton.edu

However, I identified a more fundamental constraint on the proposed delayed-choice operation.

The stoichiometric memory-capacity bound

Suppose every primary fragment AAA must be processed before the identity of its future tertiary coupling partner BBB is known.

Each Fe(OEP) molecule stores at most one primary alkyl fragment in the proposed Fe–C state. Therefore, at the instant the future partner is selected,

Nstored A≤NFe,active.\boxed{N_{\mathrm{stored}\ A}\leq N_{\mathrm{Fe,active}}.}Nstored A​≤NFe,active​.​

If the iron loading is 10 mol% relative to the amount of primary precursor, at most 10% of the initial precursor inventory can be held as intact Fe–alkyl simultaneously.

A later single readout can therefore produce at most that amount of delayed-choice coupled product, even with perfect storage and quantitative SH2S_H2SH​2 chemistry.

To process an entire batch after its precursor supply has disappeared, the architecture requires either approximately stoichiometric storage capacity or repeated transfer of precursor into a larger reservoir.

This is not a limitation on ordinary catalytic turnover. A catalyst can turn over many times when fresh precursor remains available. It is specifically a limit on how much molecular identity can be retained across a period when the precursor is no longer available.

The published Fe(OEP) reaction used 10 mol% iron in its standard conditions, with reactions commonly illuminated for 24 hours. It establishes multiple catalytic turnovers, but not a stoichiometric inventory of persistent Fe–alkyl.

macmillan.princeton.edu

This changes the intended invention: Fe(OEP) is more promising as a short-lived, regenerable reaction-state buffer than as a bulk chemical warehouse.

A useful new operation would need to exploit that buffering to control reaction timing, incompatible chemical environments or conditional product choice in a way that a comparably equipped simultaneous reactor cannot simply reproduce.

2. An experimentally grounded alternative: Separate the activation energy from the coupling event

A more useful primary result changes the direction of the construction.

In the supporting experiments to Liu and colleagues' 2021 Science paper, an independently prepared n-butyl–Fe(OEP) complex was reacted with a tertiary radical generated chemically, using zinc, zinc chloride and a redox-active ester.

The researchers conducted matched trials under light and in darkness.

macmillan.princeton.edu

Stoichiometric coupling condition

Reported product yields

Dark

40%, 44%, 49%

Illuminated

49%, 40%, 37%

The dark condition produced an average reported yield of 44.3%, compared with 42.0% under illumination. These small samples do not establish light independence universally or a statistically resolved difference between conditions.

They do establish something chemically significant:

A preformed Fe–alkyl species can be consumed in a carbon–carbon bond-forming reaction without simultaneously illuminating both coupling partners.

The experiment used approximately 0.015 mmol of preformed Fe–alkyl, five equivalents of redox-active ester, fifty equivalents of zinc and twenty-five equivalents of zinc chloride, relative to that Fe–alkyl amount, in a mixed acetone/water/benzene reaction environment.

This was a mechanistic, stoichiometric experiment, not an economical manufacturing cycle.

Nevertheless, it establishes two distinct chemical operations within one demonstrated reading environment: possession of a stored organoiron fragment and chemically driven consumption of that fragment by a subsequently generated radical.

That is substantially stronger evidence than our previous hypothetical near-quantitative kinetic regime.

The proposed differentiated operation

I am narrowing the target to dark-stage selection and coupling of chemically stored carbon fragments.

The envisioned sequence is to prepare Fe–A while the primary precursor is available, remove that precursor and its incompatible activation reagents, preserve Fe–A, and subsequently choose and generate a tertiary radical B∙B^\bulletB∙ without requiring the original photoactivation conditions.

The potential benefit is not higher intrinsic SH2S_H2SH​2 selectivity. It is the possibility of applying a later reaction environment to a fragment prepared earlier under different conditions, potentially allowing transformations that fail when all reagents and activation processes coexist.

Conventional flow synthesis can also stage incompatible reagents, so this does not yet establish a unique manufacturing advantage. The distinct chemical capability would require showing that the intermediate carries useful reactive inventory across the separation, rather than merely storing a precursor that an ordinary flow process could activate equally well later.

The 2021 experiment supports dark readout but does not demonstrate a complete write–hold–read–regenerate cycle under one common solvent and additive regime. That boundary remains open.

3. A physical reason to separate energy delivery from bond formation

The 2021 Science study contains another result especially relevant to this architecture.

Its authors observed that increasing Fe(OEP) concentration could reduce the photoredox reaction rate, even though iron was the catalyst required for selective bond formation.

Mechanistic analysis identified the cause: Fe(OEP) strongly absorbs the 450 nm light needed by the iridium photocatalyst. In the investigated regime, iron therefore competes for photons instead of increasing useful photochemical activation. The researchers reduced iron loading to 2 mol% while retaining useful catalytic performance.

PMC

This exposes a physical conflict between two desirable properties:

  • High iron concentration increases the potential capacity for storing organoiron fragments.

  • High iron concentration can decrease the fraction of incident photons that activate the separate photocatalyst.

An optical constraint

For an idealized, uniformly mixed absorbing solution, the number of photons absorbed by the productive photocatalyst is

IPC=I0αPCαPC+αFe[1−e−(αPC+αFe)L],I_{\mathrm{PC}}= I_0 \frac{\alpha_{\mathrm{PC}}} {\alpha_{\mathrm{PC}}+\alpha_{\mathrm{Fe}}} \left[ 1-e^{-(\alpha_{\mathrm{PC}}+\alpha_{\mathrm{Fe}})L} \right],IPC​=I0​αPC​+αFe​αPC​​[1−e−(αPC​+αFe​)L],

where αPC\alpha_{\mathrm{PC}}αPC​ and αFe\alpha_{\mathrm{Fe}}αFe​ are the absorption coefficients and LLL is the illuminated optical path.

If iron absorption dominates, increasing the storage capacity can decrease useful photocatalyst excitation. This is a direct radiative-transfer consequence, not an assumed chemical kinetic advantage.

The dark SH2S_H2SH​2 experiment suggests a way to eliminate that particular coupling:

Proposed energy-separated chemical cycle

WRITE — reductive activation

\(\mathrm\xrightarrowFe^I \xrightarrowFe^-A})

Store a primary alkyl fragment without requiring simultaneous tertiary-radical generation.

HOLD — reactive inventory

Maintain Fe–A and remove or terminate interfering first-stage reagents. Thermal homolysis, solvent compatibility and site exchange remain constraints.

READ — chemically generated radical

RAEB+e−→B∙+CO2+⋯\mathrm{RAE_B + e^-\rightarrow B^\bullet+CO_2+\cdots}RAEB​+e−→B∙+CO2​+⋯

FeIII−A+B∙→AB+FeII\mathrm{Fe^{III}-A+B^\bullet\rightarrow AB+Fe^{II}}FeIII−A+B∙→AB+FeII

The carbon–carbon bond-forming event need not require incident blue photons.

RESET — catalyst reduction

Regenerate active Fe(I) for another primary-alkyl loading operation, while accounting for consumed reducing equivalents and accumulated byproducts.

Each type of chemistry has experimental precedent. Their continuous repetition as one integrated, compatible operation has not been established.

Electrochemical generation of reduced iron porphyrins and subsequent alkylation has been studied since Lexa, Mispelter and Savéant's 1981 work. The 2024 Pace paper independently verifies Fe(I)-mediated primary-mesylate loading, while the 2021 Liu experiments establish dark radical coupling from preformed alkyliron.

researchgate.net
+2

However, the write and read demonstrations used different chemical environments. The 2024 independent Fe(I)-loading experiment used a strong chemical reductant in deuterated THF; the 2021 dark radical-readout experiment used zinc, zinc chloride and an acetone/water/benzene mixture.

I therefore cannot yet call this a same-medium catalytic cycle.

The most useful feature, if compatible, is not conventional photocaging. It is independent routing of electrical or chemical reducing power into separate reaction states, with the Fe–C intermediate connecting them.

That would permit a reaction requiring reductive activation of AAA to be completed using a different activation process for BBB, without sustaining both sets of activation conditions simultaneously.

The price is considerable: additional electron delivery, material handling, solvent management and possibly stoichiometric organoiron inventory.

There is also a strong existing alternative. A thin-path flow photoreactor can reduce optical screening while retaining the simultaneous iron/photoredox mechanism. Any claimed efficiency gain must beat that optimized configuration, not merely an optically thick batch reactor.

4. Two independent survival requirements

Existing organoiron measurements constrain the proposed intermediate.

Riordan and Halpern's 1996 experiments found substantially different Fe–C bond dissociation activation enthalpies for different alkyl groups, including approximately 23 kcal/mol for methyl, 19 kcal/mol for ethyl and 17 kcal/mol for neopentyl substituents. They also observed accelerated homolysis upon addition of certain axial ligands.

ScienceDirect

These measurements do not give the actual storage lifetime of the proposed n-butyl–Fe(OEP) complex in its intended mixed reaction medium. Activation enthalpies alone cannot determine a lifetime without corresponding activation entropies or measured rate constants.

They do show that the identity of the stored carbon fragment matters substantially.

More importantly, Song and Goff directly reported alkyl-group transfer between different iron porphyrins through radical-mediated exchange chemistry.

ScienceDirect

That means a fragment may survive while its association with a particular iron centre does not.

We should treat the states separately:

FeA−R⇌FeA+R∙\mathrm{Fe_A-R \rightleftharpoons Fe_A+R^\bullet}FeA​−R⇌FeA​+R∙

followed by either recapture at the original site,

FeA+R∙→FeA−R,\mathrm{Fe_A+R^\bullet\rightarrow Fe_A-R},FeA​+R∙→FeA​−R,

or capture elsewhere,

FeB+R∙→FeB−R.\mathrm{Fe_B+R^\bullet\rightarrow Fe_B-R}.FeB​+R∙→FeB​−R.

Neither necessarily destroys the stored organic fragment. Only the second destroys its original site association.

An experiment must therefore measure both the total surviving Fe–alkyl inventory and its distribution between distinguishable iron environments. Ordinary product isotope recovery cannot establish site memory.

A useful exact exchange prediction

For two equivalent address sites undergoing symmetric exchange at rate kxk_xkx​, with the organic fragment otherwise conserved, the probability of retaining the original site is

Poriginal(t)=1+e−2kxt2.\boxed{ P_{\rm original}(t)=\frac{1+e^{-2k_xt}}{2}. }Poriginal​(t)=21+e−2kx​t​.​

This is a two-state exchange-model result, not a measured Fe(OEP) law.

It predicts convergence to 50% original-site association even while 100% of the fragments could remain chemically stored.

Therefore a homogeneous catalyst population could be suitable for retaining one common building block, yet fundamentally unsuitable for routing individually assigned building blocks to predetermined reaction locations.

No immobilization or cage should be introduced until that distinction is experimentally resolved.

5. A no-go result for arbitrary addressing in a homogeneous reactor

The problem becomes sharper when multiple intended partners coexist.

Suppose two catalyst-bound fragments A1,A2A_1,A_2A1​,A2​ and two radicals B1,B2B_1,B_2B1​,B2​ are freely mixed. Their desired products are A1B1A_1B_1A1​B1​ and A2B2A_2B_2A2​B2​.

If the relevant bimolecular substitution coefficients are equal,

rij=kXibj.r_{ij}=kX_i b_j.rij​=kXi​bj​.

With equal amounts of A1,A2A_1,A_2A1​,A2​ and B1,B2B_1,B_2B1​,B2​,

r11+r22∑i,jrij=12.\frac{r_{11}+r_{22}}{\sum_{i,j}r_{ij}} =\frac12.∑i,j​rij​r11​+r22​​=21​.

Even perfectly persistent Fe–A bonds cannot recover which BBB belongs to which AAA. The required pairing information is absent from the homogeneous reaction state.

Fe–C persistence is therefore insufficient for independently addressable chemistry.

This is a genuine distinction between storing a reagent and storing an instruction. A chemically encoded instruction would require a recognition interaction, a physical address, or a timed external choice that correlates the intended partners.

Timed feeding is a legitimate solution—but an existing flow reactor can also use timed feeding. A new architecture must retain some benefit after giving that comparator identical scheduling control.

This narrows the first credible operation to delayed choice of one subsequent partner for a stored fragment population, rather than arbitrary assembly of many individually paired reactants.

6. Closing the cycle: What the evidence permits

The proposed sequence must satisfy five linked conditions.

Stage

Supported chemistry

Remaining physical requirement

Load Fe–A

Fe(I) reacts with primary electrophiles, including mesylates

macmillan.princeton.edu

Reproducible loading in a medium compatible with subsequent steps

Preserve Fe–A

Alkyliron intermediates can be observed; reversible homolysis and crossover are established

ScienceDirect

Adequate irreversible-loss lifetime and, where necessary, site retention

Generate the radical

Zinc-mediated reduction of the selected redox-active ester has produced tertiary-radical coupling under dark conditions

macmillan.princeton.edu

Controlled radical flux without destructive reactions involving Fe–A

Form and release product

Dark SH2S_H2SH​2-consistent product formation observed at 40–49% yield in the stoichiometric test

macmillan.princeton.edu

Sufficient selectivity and throughput against the strongest dark reaction alternatives

Regenerate catalyst

The established SH2S_H2SH​2 cycle produces Fe(II)

PMC

Restore Fe(I), reload AAA, and repeat without accumulating inhibition or losing active iron

A particularly important electron-balance fact is that the dark SH2S_H2SH​2 step returns Fe(II), not the Fe(I) required for the selected primary-mesylate writing pathway.

A new reducing operation is therefore necessary before another write. In addition, reduction of the redox-active ester consumes reducing equivalents and produces decarboxylation-derived waste.

The zinc experiment does not solve that full regeneration problem merely because its desired carbon–carbon product forms.

7. The discriminating physical experiment

The most informative next chemical experiment is not a larger yield optimization.

It is a delayed-choice crossover and turnover experiment using independently characterized Fe(OEP)–alkyl.

The initial Fe–alkyl population should be measured quantitatively. After selected dark holding intervals, the remaining Fe–alkyl should be measured before introducing a tertiary-radical precursor. This directly separates storage survival from readout efficiency.

The subsequent readout should compare chemically generated tertiary radicals in darkness against the best demonstrated conventional iron/photoredox reaction using the same intended coupling partners wherever their precursor compatibility permits.

Two differently labelled primary fragments would distinguish actual irreversible organic-fragment loss from transfer between metal centres. Suitable controls would establish label neutrality and distinguish site exchange from free radical release followed by recapture.

Finally, a second complete cycle must begin with the Fe(II) recovered from readout—not fresh Fe(OEP) added to replace a depleted catalyst population.

An especially informative failure would be substantial first-cycle product formation combined with an inability to reload active iron. That would establish useful stoichiometric reaction chemistry but reject repeated operation under the chosen conditions.

8. Does this outperform current chemistry?

The strongest existing comparison is no longer freely mixing radicals.

The 2021 Fe(OEP) work already supplies radical sorting and dark stoichiometric readout. The 2024 Fe/photoredox method joins primary electrophiles to tertiary bromides with useful catalytic yields. The 2026 recyclable photocatalytic system expands the range of usable precursor classes. And established reductive cross-couplings already permit staged reagent addition, including iron-mediated reactions with redox-active esters and organozinc reagents.

PMC
+3

Accordingly, the new architecture has no demonstrated generic advantage in cross-coupling yield, material economy, catalyst turnover or synthesis time.

Its potential advantage is narrower and more defensible: a stored reactive fragment could survive transfer from one activation environment into another while remaining selectively available for a partner chosen after the first activation process has ended.

That becomes consequential only when at least one of the following is established within an actual reaction family: simultaneous exposure destroys a valuable substrate, an activation reagent inhibits an essential downstream step, or optical/redox interactions prevent productive operation at a useful concentration.

The present primary evidence does not yet establish such an advantage for the same target product under matched conditions.

Scientific checkpoint

This investigation has produced a more specific principle than generic partner-selective confinement:

Orthogonal energy delivery can, in principle, separate creation of an organometallic reactive inventory from its subsequent bond-forming consumption. Fe(OEP) offers experimentally established building blocks for testing that separation.

The new substantive boundaries are the stoichiometric inventory limit, photon-absorption competition, distinct fragment/site memory, the homogeneous-addressing limitation, and the requirement to regenerate Fe(I) after dark SH2S_H2SH​2 readout.

The strongest unresolved chemical question is now whether an Fe–alkyl state can carry useful carbon-fragment inventory across a genuine change of chemical activation conditions, with enough survival and regeneration to outperform a directly staged reaction using the same resources.

If this fails, the correct next move is to change the organometallic storage chemistry, not to assign better rates or add an unsubstantiated host. Cobalamin-derived organocobalt systems are a relevant alternative because recent primary work has demonstrated solvent- and radical-trap-dependent Co–C photochemistry, but their compatibility with this full carbon–carbon manufacturing cycle would require a separate construction.

pubs.rsc.org

The branch remains at a constructive chemical hypothesis supported by real component reactions, with an identified operating principle and an experimentally resolvable boundary. No integrated new manufacturing operation has yet been demonstrated.

7. The discriminating physical experiment

The most informative next chemical experiment is not a larger yield optimization.

It is a delayed-choice crossover and turnover experiment using independently characterized Fe(OEP)–alkyl.

The initial Fe–alkyl population should be measured quantitatively. After selected dark holding intervals, the remaining Fe–alkyl should be measured before introducing a tertiary-radical precursor. This directly separates storage survival from readout efficiency.

The subsequent readout should compare chemically generated tertiary radicals in darkness against the best demonstrated conventional iron/photoredox reaction using the same intended coupling partners wherever their precursor compatibility permits.

Two differently labelled primary fragments would distinguish actual irreversible organic-fragment loss from transfer between metal centres. Suitable controls would establish label neutrality and distinguish site exchange from free radical release followed by recapture.

Finally, a second complete cycle must begin with the Fe(II) recovered from readout—not fresh Fe(OEP) added to replace a depleted catalyst population.

An especially informative failure would be substantial first-cycle product formation combined with an inability to reload active iron. That would establish useful stoichiometric reaction chemistry but reject repeated operation under the chosen conditions.
